title: Inside the American ghost town where stolen souvenirs lead to ruin
excerpt: Legend warns that anyone who takes even a rock, nail or speck of dust will be plagued by terrible misfortune.
content:
The abandoned Gold Rush town of Bodie is said to be one of the most cursed places in America.

According to local legend, anyone who removes so much as a rock, nail or speck of dust from the California ghost town will be struck by terrible misfortune.

Visitors have blamed stolen souvenirs for car accidents, severe illnesses, lost jobs and years of turmoil.

Some became so frightened that they mailed the objects back, accompanied by desperate letters begging the town for forgiveness.

Park employees have received so many of the confessions that a collection of them has been displayed in the Bodie museum.

One visitor admitted that their trail of misfortune was so long and depressing that they could not bear to list it.

Others warned that their lives began to unravel only after they dismissed the curse as harmless folklore.

But the sinister legend may have been created by a park ranger to frighten tourists into leaving the town's historic treasures untouched.

Anyone who takes home anything from the town falls victim to terrible ill luck

Bodie stands in the Bodie Hills, east of the Sierra Nevada mountain range and close to California's border with Nevada.

The former mining settlement is now preserved in a state of 'arrested decay,' with buildings stabilized but not restored and interiors maintained largely as they were left by their last occupants.

The town is also reputedly haunted by several ghosts, including a Chinese woman, a mysterious figure who peers from an upstairs window and a little girl whose laughter can supposedly be heard in the cemetery.

Kieron Connolly, author of Abandoned Places, a book about some of the world's most mysterious abandoned locations, said Bodie's eerie emptiness made it fertile ground for supernatural stories.

Connolly told the Daily Mail: 'Whether you believe in the curse or not, you can see how the eerie emptiness of Bodie lends itself to the supernatural.

'We expect towns to get bigger and busier and to be modernised. When we see somewhere that time has forgotten, unpopulated and left behind, we find it a bit unsettling - but fascinating.'

The letters sent back to Bodie offer chilling accounts from visitors who claim their troubles began after they removed objects from the town.

One, sent in 2004 with a collection of rocks, reads: 'You can have these godforsaken rocks back. I've never had so much rotten luck in my life. Please forgive me for ever testing the curse of Bodie.'

By 1881, Reverend F.M. Warrington described the town as 'A sea of sin, lashed by the tempests of lust and passion.'

Another visitor returned a shoe taken decades earlier.

'Please find enclosed one weather-beaten old shoe. The shoe was removed from Bodie during the month of August 1978... My trail of misfortune is so long and depressing it can't be listed here,' the letter reads.

Even people who took seemingly worthless objects, including old nails and scraps of metal, later blamed them for a sudden run of bad luck.

One letter sent in 2003 said, 'Dear Bodie... I'm sorry that I took this piece of metal from the town. I thought it was all a joke, but it wasn't at all. Things are happening that are very hard to explain.'

Another, dated 1998, said, 'So sorry for picking these up. I love antiques and being a Christian I felt so guilty for taking these on Monday. Not to mention Tuesday we got a flat tire and my husband hit his head on a rock.'

A visitor writing in 2002 issued an ominous warning to anyone tempted to test the legend.

'Fair warning for anyone that thinks this is just folklore -- my life has never seen such turmoil. Please take my warning and do not remove even a speck of dust.'

The stream of returned objects became so regular that park employees reportedly learned to recognize the packages when collecting Bodie's mail.

The 'curse' itself is even more mysterious, with ill luck said to befall anyone who takes anything, no matter how small, from the town

Connolly said, 'By 1940 the population was down to 40. Today, Bodie is maintained in a state of arrested decay as a visitor attraction.'

However, California State Parks warns that returned objects create additional problems for the site.

Employees may be unable to prove that an item genuinely came from Bodie or determine its original location, meaning it cannot necessarily be placed back inside the park.

Processing the objects is also time-consuming, and park interpreter Catherine Jones said in 2018 that employees had to file a law-enforcement report for every returned item, regardless of its size.

Taking the objects is not merely an invitation for supernatural revenge - it is illegal.

California regulations prohibit visitors from removing rocks or disturbing objects of archaeological or historical interest inside state parks.

Officials also ask visitors not to pick up and move objects because Bodie is effectively a vast outdoor museum whose artifacts help tell the town's story.

Long before it became associated with ghosts and curses, Bodie was one of California's most notorious boomtowns.

Gold was discovered there in 1859 by W.S. Bodey, who died in a blizzard that same year while attempting to return to the site.

It remains unclear whether the town's altered spelling resulted from a mistake or an attempt to make its pronunciation clearer.

Connolly said, 'Gold was discovered at Bodie in 1859 (just after the initial California gold rush), and it went from mining camp to boomtown.'

Mining initially progressed slowly as richer discoveries elsewhere drew prospectors away.

But in the mid-1870s, the Bunker Hill Mine, later renamed the Standard Mining Company, struck a rich deposit of gold and silver ore.

The discovery triggered a rush, and by 1879 Bodie had approximately 8,500 residents and more than 2,000 buildings, according to California State Parks.

At its height, the town resembled something from a Western, with more than 60 saloons and dance halls lining its streets.

Gunfights, stagecoach robberies and street brawls helped give rise to the legend of the 'Bad Man of Bodie,' although historians believe the supposed outlaw was likely a composite of several lawless residents.

Bodie also had a sizeable Chinese community numbering several hundred people.

Its Chinatown contained general stores, laundries, boarding houses, gambling halls, saloons and a Taoist temple.

Chinese residents were largely excluded from white society and built what California State Parks describes as a 'town within the town,' where they could preserve their customs and traditions.

In 1881, Reverend F.M. Warrington described Bodie as 'A sea of sin, lashed by the tempests of lust and passion.'

But the boom did not last.

Connolly said, 'Its decline began in 1880, when word spread of new boomtowns elsewhere. The Standard Consolidated Mine closed in 1913, and four years later the Bodie Railway was abandoned.'

The town was already in decline by 1881 as rich deposits were exhausted, mining companies failed and residents departed for more profitable areas.

Its population had fallen to approximately 1,500 by 1886.

Fires subsequently destroyed much of Bodie, including a major blaze in 1932, and the settlement faded into a ghost town during the 1940s.

Others have warned visitors against taking even the smallest items from the town

Connolly said, 'By 1940 the population was down to 40. Today, Bodie is maintained in a state of arrested decay as a visitor attraction.'

The surviving portion of the town became a California State Historic Park in 1962 and was designated a National Historic Landmark.

Its deserted homes and violent past eventually spawned stories of restless spirits.

The J.S. Cain House is said to be haunted by a Chinese woman who reportedly dislikes adults but is fond of children.

Stories claim adults sleeping in the house have felt an invisible weight pressing down on them, while doors have allegedly opened and closed on their own.

The Dechambeau House is said to be visited by the apparition of a woman who peers from an upstairs window.

Bodie's cemetery is also associated with the ghost of Evelyn Myers, known as the 'Angel of Bodie.'

The three-year-old died in April 1897 after being accidentally struck in the head with a pickaxe while a worker was digging a drainage ditch near her family's home.

Her grave is marked by a white marble angel, and legend holds that her laughter can still be heard around the cemetery.

The origins of the Bodie Curse are more recent, and apparently less supernatural.

Jones told KQED in 2018 that a lone park ranger had created the story years earlier in an attempt to stop visitors from stealing artifacts.

The abandoned Gold Rush town of Bodie in California is among America's most mysterious

'Years back,' says Jones, a single park ranger at Bodie apparently invented the notion that misfortune would befall anyone who took something from the park. 'That maybe if we started this idea that you'd have bad luck if you took artifacts from Bodie, it would try to keep people from stealing artifacts.'

Theft had plagued Bodie even before it became a state park, with one person reportedly removing an entire piano from the abandoned town and driving away with it.

That piano was eventually returned and placed inside Bodie's Odd Fellows Hall.

But the strategy intended to protect the town had an unintended consequence.

Instead of simply discouraging theft, the legend apparently convinced visitors that returning stolen objects could reverse their misfortune, creating a steady flow of rocks, nails, glass and other items through the mail.

Skeptics say coincidence, guilt and the human tendency to connect unrelated events offer more likely explanations for the accidents, illnesses and other calamities described in the letters.

California State Parks now emphasizes the damage caused by removing artifacts rather than promoting the curse.

Officials warn that when an object is taken, part of Bodie's history disappears with it, and mailing it back may not repair the harm.

Yet the letters continue to provide an ominous warning to anyone tempted to test the legend.

Whether the curse is supernatural or a remarkably effective piece of park folklore, many visitors have decided it is safer not to take the chance.
